value.overview: The Collared Aracari (Pteroglossus torquatus) is a colorful small toucan of tropical Central and northern South America. It has a long, serrated bill, yellow underparts, dark wings and back, a red rump, and a dark collar-like band across the upper breast. It commonly travels in small groups through forest canopies, feeding on fruit and other food. In Costa Rica, it is an important resident toucan of lowland forests, forest edges, and connected wooded habitats.
value.classification: The Collared Aracari belongs to the toucan family Ramphastidae and the order Piciformes. It is one of the smaller aracaris in the genus Pteroglossus.
value.identification: This aracari is about 38–41 cm long and has a mostly blackish back, bright yellow underparts, red markings on the rump and belly, and a dark band across the upper breast. Its large bill is pale or whitish on the upper portion, darker below, and has tooth-like serrations along the cutting edge. The skin around the eye and bill is reddish, and the eyes are yellow. Females generally have a shorter bill than males. It may be confused with the Fiery-billed Aracari in Costa Rica, but range is useful for identification.
value.rangeHabitat: The Collared Aracari ranges from eastern and southern Mexico through Central America to northern South America, including Colombia and Venezuela. In Costa Rica, it is a resident and is most common in lowlands and foothills of the Caribbean slope, locally reaching about 1,000–1,200 m. It also occurs on the northern Pacific slope, where it is generally less common and local; the central and southern Pacific region is mainly occupied by the Fiery-billed Aracari. It uses mature and secondary forest, forest edges, gallery forest, cacao and other plantations, and wooded clearings.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally nonmigratory. It makes local movements while following fruiting trees and may visit gardens, plantations, and forest edges, but it is not known for regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: The Collared Aracari nests in a natural tree cavity or an old cavity made by a woodpecker. The pair may enlarge and clean the cavity before breeding. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young, and other group members may assist with feeding in some populations. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been recorded mainly during the first half of the year, with nesting observations extending from roughly January or February into May or June. Clutches commonly contain about three eggs, although details may vary geographically.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the main part of the diet, including soft fruits and the fleshy portions of palm fruits. The aracari also eats seeds, insects and other small invertebrates, and may take eggs or nestlings of other birds. It usually feeds in the canopy, moving actively through fruiting trees in groups. It may also visit farms, gardens, and plantations where bananas, plantains, cacao, or other suitable foods are available.
value.behavior: Collared Aracaris are social and are often seen in groups of approximately 6–15 birds, although individuals or pairs may travel alone. They move through the canopy with quick hops and short flights, and their direct flight across clearings makes their long tail and large bill conspicuous. Groups may roost together in a tree cavity, sometimes sharing a cavity with a breeding pair. Their calls are sharp, squeaky, or rasping notes, often given while birds are moving through the canopy.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species is not currently assessed as threatened with extinction.
